canonical_definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats problem-solving ability as a broad capability to solve complex or unfamiliar tasks by devising and executing a strategy toward a goal or correct answer. Many definitions keep this general, describing the capacity to handle challenging situations, solve tasks across disciplines, or be "capable of generalized problem solving as humans do." A smaller line of work narrows the term to competitive mathematics that requires non-trivial insight, to tool-aided task solving, or to multimodal settings where text and images must be integrated, and some authors define it more directly through benchmark performance, distinguishing it from data generation ability and from error detection.

Space of facets. Papers do not present a single formal taxonomy, but they do use adjacent labels such as generalized problem solving, problem-solving capability, and multimodal problem solving. The construct is frequently positioned alongside reasoning-focused concepts: algorithmic reasoning is said to play a role in problem-solving, and mathematical reasoning is described as a benchmark for advanced reasoning and problem-solving abilities. Some papers also separate it from neighboring capacities, treating it as different from data generation ability and, when a gold answer is provided, from error detection.

Space of measurement. It is linked to 4 measurement instruments and 2 behavioral indicators. The measurement space is centered on question-based benchmarks, with MMLU used most often, followed by MMLU-Pro, MathQA, and PutnamBench; papers describe these as gauging general problem-solving across diverse subjects, testing real-world text understanding and complex problem solving, testing numerical reasoning in word problems, and requiring broad mathematical proficiency. These operationalizations mostly treat the construct as success on challenging tasks, while some definitions frame it more as devising and executing a solution strategy.

Links. Papers also link the construct to 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. One paper claims a causal relationship from self-improvement to problem-solving ability, describing post-training self-improvement as enhancing problem-solving capabilities, and the same line of work also claims a causal relationship from self-correction to problem-solving ability, while noting that post-prompting strategies are limited by intrinsic self-correction capabilities. Separately, one paper reports that error localization is weakly correlated with problem-solving ability, and papers describe algorithmic reasoning and mathematical reasoning as related to it.

relationships.evidence: Algorithmic reasoning is a fundamental cognitive ability that plays a pivotal role in problem-solving and decision-making processes. (Abstract)

relationships.paper: PutnamBench: Evaluating Neural Theorem-Provers on the Putnam Mathematical Competition
relationships.evidence: PUTNAMBENCH requires significant problem-solving ability and proficiency in a broad range of topics taught in undergraduate mathematics courses.

relationships.paper: Progress or Regress? Self-Improvement Reversal in Post-training
relationships.evidence: Self-improvement through post-training methods such as iterative preference learning has been acclaimed for enhancing the problem-solving capabilities (e.g., mathematical reasoning) of Large Language Models (LLMs) without human intervention. (ABSTRACT)

iclr25: Progress or Regress? Self-Improvement Reversal in Post-training

relationships.paper: Progress or Regress? Self-Improvement Reversal in Post-training
relationships.evidence: ...post-prompting strategies are limited by the model’s intrinsic self-correction capabilities, thereby failing to significantly enhance problem-solving capabilities. (Section 2)

iclr25: Progress or Regress? Self-Improvement Reversal in Post-training

relationships.paper: LLMs cannot spot math errors, even when allowed to peek into the solution
relationships.evidence: A chi-squared test for independence confirms that error localization and problem-solving accuracy are weakly correlated (p > 0.01; ϕ < 0.2) across models and prompts (Section 4.2)

emnlp25: LLMs cannot spot math errors, even when allowed to peek into the solution

relationships.paper: Warm Up Before You Train: Unlocking General Reasoning in Resource-Constrained Settings
relationships.evidence: MMLU-Pro: An enhanced version of the Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) benchmark, featuring challenging questions across 14 categories like physics, law, history, and so on to test real-world text understanding and complex problem solving (Section 2.2)

emnlp25: Warm Up Before You Train: Unlocking General Reasoning in Resource-Constrained Settings

relationships.paper: NESTFUL: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on Nested Sequences of API Calls
relationships.evidence: It consists of questions that test numerical reasoning and problem-solving skills, requiring models to both understand the text of a word problem and perform mathematical operations to arrive at the correct solution. (Section 3.2.1)

emnlp25: NESTFUL: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on Nested Sequences of API Calls

relationships.paper: SBSC: Step-by-Step Coding for Improving Mathematical Olympiad Performance
relationships.evidence: Mathematical reasoning has emerged as a critical benchmark to measure the advanced reasoning and problem-solving abilities of the Large Language Models (LLMs) (Section 1).

iclr25: SBSC: Step-by-Step Coding for Improving Mathematical Olympiad Performance
